🎙
Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman
Maria Zakharova
’s
answer
to a media question regarding the Latvian government’s plans to adopt a “de-Russification declaration”
(November 27, 2026)
❓
Question:
The Latvian authorities intend to adopt a “de-Russification declaration,” which envisages establishing a legal basis for restricting the use of the Russian language in the public space. The Latvian government also intends to toughen penalties for violations of the law on the state language. How would you comment on this initiative?
💬
Maria Zakharova:
The recent anti-Russian statements by Latvian officials once again highlight their Russophobic nature. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’s assertion that Riga is not ready to normalise relations with our country “even after a ceasefire in Ukraine” is
no revelation
– the entire policy pursued by that country’s authorities in recent years clearly and unequivocally points to this. Take, for example, the government’s fresh plans to deal yet another blow to the country’s Russian-speaking residents by adopting the
“de-Russification declaration.”
The Russian language has always been Riga’s sworn enemy, and
the protracted war against it is now taking on a new dimension.
The Latvian authorities are striving to restrict still further the scope for using it in the country, even though communicating in Russian is already forbidden in schools, higher education institutions and workplaces.
All Russian-speaking inhabitants of Latvia are regarded by this repressive regime as nothing more than potential “public enemies,” to say nothing of those who dare to openly express their dissatisfaction with the authorities’ policies or do not hide their “dissent” on the subject of Russia. Their prospects in today’s Latvia boil down to a simple formula:
either deportation or prison.
<...>
Latvia’s Russophobic authorities continue their
campaign against Soviet military memorials.
Justifying their shameful actions with the myth of the “Soviet occupation,” they have already demolished more than 200 Soviet military memorials <...>.
Another recent
anti-Russian outrage
by the Latvian authorities is their plan to force the dismissal of the staff of the Social Welfare Department at the Russian Embassy in Riga, which will make it impossible to pay pensions to Russian military pensioners living in Latvia – for many, their
only source of income.
<...>
Official Riga actively positions itself as one of the most zealous allies of the Kiev regime. Leading, together with Britain, the International Drone Coalition, it has already handed
over tens of thousands of UAVs
to the Ukrainian Armed Forces for carrying out regular attacks on Russian territory. <...>
NATO formations regularly hold exercises in the country, and the Alliance’s permanent military presence is expanding, creating additional threats along our western borders. The potential adversary in these exercises is named openly – manoeuvres are being rehearsed for
conducting combat operations against Russia.
<...>
Lacking the legal grounds to outright ban the transit of Russian grain across its territory, which serves
the interests of developing countries,
Riga is creating artificial obstacles to impede as far as possible the prompt delivery of Russian grain to world markets, thereby further increasing the risks to global food security. <...>.
The current Latvian authorities, of course, have
no desire for any normalisation of relations with Russia;
on the contrary, they constantly pursue a path of ever-greater escalation, even to the point of
provoking open conflict.
<...>
☝️
This is not our choice,
but we cannot ignore the threats,
and we reserve the right to take resolute retaliatory measures of a political and diplomatic nature to reliably safeguard Russia’s national interests and the rights of its citizens.

These documents vividly illustrate the key milestones of multifaceted Russian-Emirati cooperation, which has now reached the level of a strategic partnership.
In his welcoming remarks,
Sergey Lavrov
emphasised that regular contacts between President

provide the main boost for bilateral cooperation. The two leaders discussed in detail current bilateral issues and global and regional issues during

on January 29, 2026.
The Minister spoke highly of
close coordination with Abu Dhabi
through the Foreign Ministries, including at international fora, as well as the
intensive exchange of delegations
at the level of executive authorities.
🤝
Sergey Lavrov
highlighted the dynamic
development of trade and economic ties,
with the Russian-Emirati Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Technical Cooperation playing a coordinating role. He underscored the important contribution of the Russian-Emirati Business Council to strengthening cooperation between the two countries’ business communities.
Sergey Lavrov drew attention to
the significant expansion of bilateral contacts
in the cultural, humanitarian and educational spheres, as well as growing tourism ties. He noted
the successful work
of the Sheikha Fatima Centre for International Cooperation with the UAE, which was officially opened at the Yevgeny Primakov Regional Gymnasium in October 2024 in the presence of the two countries’ leaders. He also noted the high-profile Russian Culture Days held in Abu Dhabi in November 2025 and the UAE Culture Days held in Moscow in August 2026.
The event was attended by UAE Ambassador to Russia
Mohammed Al Jaber,
heads of diplomatic missions accredited in Moscow, members of both chambers of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation, and representatives of Russia’s academic and expert communities.

🎙
Remarks
by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at the opening of an exhibition marking the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Russia and the United Arab Emirates
(Moscow, 27 November 2026)
💬
Sergey Lavrov:
The UAE is
a truly strategic partner
for Russia. Our cooperation rests on equality, mutual respect and regard for each other’s national interests. It offers
a good example
of how states can work together as equals in a
#MultipolarWorld
.
The close friendship between our countries goes back many years. On 8 December 1971, just days after the formation of the UAE was announced,
the Soviet Union recognised the new state and expressed its readiness to establish diplomatic relations with it
.
Since then,
our ties have developed steadily
, and the pace of cooperation across a wide range of fields has picked up year by year.
The Declaration on Strategic Partnership between the Russian Federation and the United Arab Emirates
, signed in Moscow on 1 June 2018, provides
a firm foundation
for this cooperation.
It is hard to overstate the importance of the regular contacts and mutual trust between our Presidents,
Vladimir Putin
and
Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan
. On 29 January, the UAE President paid
another visit to Moscow
, where the two Leaders
discussed the full range of bilateral issues in detail
, along with key issues on the global and regional agenda.
Our Foreign Ministries coordinate closely
, including in international forums. Other government agencies also regularly exchange delegations. I recently took part once again in the prestigious
Sir Bani Yas Forum
in Abu Dhabi, where
I held talks
with my colleague and friend
Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan
.
📈
Our trade and economic ties are growing rapidly
. Last year,
bilateral trade rose by 56%
, reaching an all-time high.
The Russia-UAE Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Technical Cooperation
plays the leading role in coordinating efforts to expand bilateral cooperation. Its next meeting is due to take place in Moscow
on December
8
. The Russia-UAE Business Council has also proved effective in forging closer ties between our business communities.
I should also mention that
the UAE is one of the most popular overseas holiday destinations for Russians
. In 2025, Russian citizens made
more than 2 million trips to the UAE
, while Emirati citizens made
more than 70,000 trips to Russia
. I am confident these figures will continue to rise. With visa-free travel in place, we have every reason to expect more tourists to travel in both directions.
🤝
We will continue to work energetically alongside our Emirati friends to take our cooperation further in every field.

🎙
Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova's
statement
regarding Russia’s alleged plans to launch a spacecraft carrying a nuclear warhead
(November 26, 2026)
💬
The Western political and expert circles continue to repeat
allegations about nuclear weapons in space
.
The latest allegations
have been published
by the German media in the form of
a “journalistic investigation”
regarding
Russia’s alleged plans to orbit a spacecraft with a nuclear warhead
in the near future for a potential mass attack on orbital satellite constellations.
The publication of this false information during a regular session of
the Open-ended Working Group on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space in all its Aspects
(OEWG on PAROS) in Geneva, established in accordance with
UNGA Decision 79/512
, is obviously
interfering with a depoliticised substantive dialogue on a platform established to address space security issues
.
☝️
But this does not bother German Russophobes.
We reiterate that these absurd allegations regarding Russia’s activities in outer space
have nothing in common with reality
and are aimed at
justifying Germany’s destructive moves to orbit weapons in space
, as well as the allocation of multibillion-euro funding for this purpose.
This concerns, in particular,
the development of the Precision Orbital Deep Strike system
by German concerns for potential deployment in low-Earth orbit, as well as
plans
announced by German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius to invest 35 billion euros
in measures to strengthen German military space capabilities by the mid-2030s.
❗️
We have pointed out on numerous occasions that the Russian Federation is conducting space exploration and development activities
in full compliance with its international obligations, exclusively for peaceful purposes, and do not threaten other states
.

⚡️
“State Sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security”
, an article by
Dmitry Medvedev
, Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of the Russian Federation, published in
the Moscow Journal of International Law
(November 23, 2026)
(
FULL ARTICLE
: Telegraph
Part 1
|
Part 2
|
Part 3
)
✍️
Developments surrounding Iran
and the ongoing debate over
Russia’s right to use nuclear weapons
in the course of
the special military operation
give us cause to ask how firmly established
the legal foundations of nuclear non-proliferation
are today, and whether they are set in stone.
Key points
:
👉
A state’s right to ensure its own survival under international law
It is worth recalling
the International Court of Justice’s 1996 advisory opinion
on
the Legality of the Use by a State of Nuclear Weapons in Armed Conflict
. The Court stated that it
“cannot lose sight of the fundamental right of every State to survival, and thus its right to resort to self-defence, in accordance with
Article 51 of the UN Charter
, when its survival is at stake.”
👉
The NPT: the limits of the treaty regime and Iran’s legal status
At various times, different legal grounds have been invoked
to justify what was, in essence, a political campaign to put pressure on Iran
. The unlawfulness of this Western approach became clearest when Western countries moved from monitoring and sanctions to the use of armed force. <…>
None of these instruments authorised the US or Israel
to use armed force as a sanction for Iran’s breach of its nuclear obligations, nor did the UN Security Council issue a separate authorisation for such an operation.
This is what distinguishes the preventive measures
Russia took as part of the special military operation under
Article 51 of the UN Charter
.
The immediate grounds for launching the special military operation were
the direct threat of military action by Ukraine
, which in 2019 declared
full NATO membership
a strategic objective and in 2020 became
a NATO Enhanced Opportunities Partner
, and
the genocide perpetrated by Ukraine against its own population
in the east of the country.
☝️
As for the other threats Russia faces as the Ukrainian crisis unfolds, Kiev and those who share its views should always bear in mind that
we have the right, and in certain circumstances the duty
, to
use all means at our disposal
to safeguard national security, including, potentially, the use of nuclear weapons.
The current version of
the Basic Principles of State Policy of the Russian Federation on Nuclear Deterrence
expressly provides for this possibility
.
👉
The limits international law places on safeguarding national security today
• On July 22, 2026, the German government issued
a contradictory statement
. It pledged to honour its obligations under
the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
(
#NPT
) and
the Two Plus Four Treaty
, while confirming that Germany would continue to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and cooperate with France on
“forward deterrence”
.
This position
blurs the legal distinction
between the prohibition on Germany manufacturing, possessing or exercising control over nuclear weapons and its growing involvement in
the alliance’s nuclear policy
.
👉
The legal foundations of nuclear non-proliferation
can hardly be regarded as immutable
. Yet it is equally clear that, at this point in history,
they are the best humanity has devised
.
What undermines the universality of the
#NPT
is
the uneven way it is applied in practice for political reasons
, rather than any flaw in the text of the Treaty.
When the nuclear activities a state is permitted to pursue depend in practice on whether it is
an adversary or an ally
of a major power or a military bloc,
the rules of the non-proliferation regime lose some of their credibility
.
In formal terms, the same law applies to all, yet
political practice makes its application selective
. Today,
this contradiction poses one of the gravest threats
to the stability of the non-proliferation regime.
📄

item.title: 🗓 On November 26, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held his traditional meeting with participants in
item.description: 🗓 On November 26, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held his traditional meeting with participants in the Dialogue for the Future programme , an annual research and educational initiative organised by the Alexander Gorchakov Public Diplomacy Fund . In an informal, interactive session with the head of Russian diplomacy, young representatives of the academic, research and expert communities of Russia and other countries exchanged views on various aspects of international relations . The discussion focused on key developments and trends of 2026. Participants in the programme examined, through the lens of the Russian school of diplomacy, the challenges of conducting negotiations amid political turbulence , as well as mechanisms for strengthening interstate dialogue .
